# APPENDICES

## Appendix A: Twenty Principles

**The distillation.** Twenty principles about how to design and diagnose systems.

Read this page first and last. It carries how to think. Appendix B carries what the options are called, and the two are meant to be used together: a principle without the vocabulary cannot pick an option, and the vocabulary without a principle cannot rank two options that both sound right.

### How to read a problem

**1. Every described situation is diagnostic, never definitional, and one fact in it does most of the eliminating.** Locate where the problem actually sits, then refuse the seven shapes a wrong answer takes: the compensating control that makes failure visible rather than impossible, the burden shift that puts a decision on the model that belongs in code, the destructive shortcut that surrenders what the situation required, the true irrelevance that is accurate about the wrong component, the vocabulary swap that substitutes an adjacent term, the invented feature that names a capability that does not exist and the structural inversion that puts content in the channel built for its opposite.

### Ownership

**2. Settle ownership before shape.** Claude, existing systems, humans. Over-assigning to Claude is the most common and most expensive early mistake, and anything the organization has already paid to make reliable keeps its job rather than having its logic reproduced.

**3. Justify every assignment on reversibility, stakes and accountability.** They move independently and any one of them can force human retention. And governance rules a route out before cost or latency are weighed at all, as a filter applied first rather than a factor balanced later.

### Shape

**4. Where the control flow lives is what names the pattern.** In your code it is a workflow and there are seams between steps where deterministic guards sit. Inside the model it is an agent and there is no code boundary where a guard can sit.

**5. Unpredictability alone does not license an agent.** The failure must also be acceptable and recoverable. Unpredictable plus unrecoverable means re-scope the work, not add monitoring.

**6. Take the simplest shape that meets the error tolerance and observability requirements**, and escalate only when measurement shows it falling short, never when it merely feels insufficient.

**7. Controls are architecture, not additions.** Scoped tools, turn budgets, explicit permissions, stopping criteria and human gates positioned by reversibility and stakes. Every control needs a defined failure behavior, safety-critical ones fail closed and sampled review is a measurement instrument rather than a safety control.

**8. Design the model's interface as carefully as a person's.** Clear tool descriptions, unambiguous parameters, output formats close to what the model has already seen and an arrangement in which the wrong call is hard to make. An agent must take ground truth from the environment at every step, because one that acts without reading the result cannot assess progress, catch its own error or adapt. Show the planning steps while it works.

### Composition and context

**9. Architectures are references, not blueprints.** Name one, then adapt it. Compose two only when the halves fail differently in ways worth managing separately, because reaching for a second pattern while the problem is still undecided is a deferral dressed as a design.

**10. The orchestrator owns the goal and never does the work.** Subagent failures are recoverable and orchestrator failures usually are not, so make subagent work idempotent, protect orchestrator state, propagate one trace end to end and give every subagent what it needs because it inherits nothing.

**11. Context is a finite resource, not a container to fill.** Attention degrades as the window grows, so the target is the smallest set of high-signal tokens that produces the outcome. Carry identifiers and fetch at runtime rather than pre-loading. When work outruns the window, compact it, write notes outside it, or hand the exploration to a subagent that returns a summary. A larger window buys room, never relevance.

### Data and integration

**12. Retrieval is for what was true yesterday and will be true tomorrow.** Live state belongs to the system that owns it and is reached by tool call. Similarity is not truth: a higher score means the text was close to the question, which stops being the same claim the moment the state changes underneath it.

**13. The corpus chooses the chunking and the queries choose the indexing.** Never a default size, never one index shape for every query shape, and ask first whether a pipeline is needed at all rather than assuming one.

**14. A chunk pulled from its document loses its bearings.** Situate each one before embedding it, run lexical alongside semantic because that single addition recovers the most, and retrieve wide then rerank down rather than retrieving narrow and hoping.

**15. Excess capability is removed, not logged, confirmed or gated.** Where the catalog is legitimately large, removal is unavailable and the answer is to defer the definitions instead. Authorization always sits outside the model.

### Models and prompting

**16. Fix the instruction before reaching for more.** More reasoning, more examples, a larger window or a bigger model are all downstream of a vague instruction, and a model choice is settled with an evaluation set rather than an argument.

**17. Structure decides what an instruction can do.** Untrusted content goes in the channel built to distrust it, your own instructions never go in that channel, and no wording turns a prompt into a control over a consequential action. That needs a code gate.

### Evaluation

**18. What you cannot see you must measure, and measure properly.** Retrieval quality is invisible in the output, each component of a composed system needs its own eval set, and a healthy aggregate reliably masks a broken segment. Prefer many automated cases to few hand-graded ones, make a grader reason before it scores, test offline before production and change one thing at a time.

**19. Distrust a system that reports health.** The failures worth designing against are fluent, confident and wrong, with normal latency, no errors and nobody positioned to notice except the person harmed. Over-refusal sits on the same ledger as a defect, not as caution.

### People

**20. Never hand over one option, one number or one document.** Alternatives with what each costs, translated to what the audience is accountable for. Commitments measurable, a stated want examined rather than accepted as a requirement, documentation recording why and not only what, handoff designed from the start and no design that leaves you a permanent dependency.

### The thread

The dangerous failure never announces itself. Settle ownership early, hold the shape as simple as the requirement allows, spend context and capability as the scarce things they are, put controls where the failure becomes impossible rather than visible and measure the thing that does not show up in the output.

**One limitation, stated plainly.** These twenty are necessary and not sufficient. They encode judgment, and judgment alone does not supply the vocabulary an option is phrased in. That is what Appendix B is for, and it is not optional.
